name: YK-11

lead: YK-11 is an experimental steroid-based compound classed as a SARM, though it behaves as a partial androgen receptor agonist. Research is confined to cell studies, mainly from Japanese groups in 2011 to 2013.
It is sold as a research chemical. No human trials exist.

paras: In cultured muscle cells it increased follistatin expression and reduced myostatin signalling via androgen receptor activation. These results have not been shown in humans.
Not approved and banned in sport. Safety is untested in humans, and liver, hormonal and cardiovascular effects are suspected. Products sold online are frequently mislabelled.

lead: YK-11 is a synthetic steroidal compound that is usually classed as a selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM). Wikipedia describes it as a gene-selective partial agonist of the androgen receptor that does not trigger the N/C interaction normally needed for full receptor activation, and as having anabolic activity in cultured C2C12 myoblasts greater than that of dihydrotestosterone (DHT).[1] It has been investigated in animal studies of sepsis-induced muscle wasting and has appeared on the market as a designer drug.[1]

The compound was reported by Yuichiro Kanno and colleagues at Toho University, Japan, around 2011, with a follow-up 2013 paper in Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin reporting that YK-11 increased follistatin expression in myoblasts, the basis of its marketing as a myostatin inhibitor.[2][3] Published work consists of cell and animal studies; no human clinical trial of YK-11 was found.[1]

YK-11 is not authorised as a medicine anywhere noted in the sources. Health Canada warned in 2022 that SARMs such as YK-11 are not authorised for any use and that bodybuilding products containing them can pose risks such as heart attack, stroke and liver damage.[1] It is on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list and has been detected in doping control samples and in dietary supplements.[2][4][5]

paras: YK-11 has no approved medical use. Wikipedia notes animal investigation for sepsis-induced muscle wasting.[1] It is sold by online vendors as a research chemical and bodybuilding product, sometimes labelled myostine, and sometimes touted in bodybuilding circles as a potent myostatin inhibitor even though it remains experimental.[1][2] T Nation posters have described cycles with it alone or alongside other SARMs, GW501516 and andarine, and a mix that dropped RAD-140 for YK-11 and andarine.[6][7][8]

No studies found. No human clinical trial of YK-11 has been published.[1] Laboratory and animal research is described under Pharmacology and Research. A published case report documented detection of YK-11 in an athlete's doping control sample, which is an analytic finding and not a treatment study.[9]

Kanno's group found that YK-11 activates the androgen receptor as a partial agonist, promoting nuclear translocation without inducing the amino/carboxyl-terminal interaction that DHT induces.[1][2] In C2C12 myoblasts, YK-11 promoted myogenic differentiation more strongly than DHT, with the 2013 paper attributing this to increased expression of follistatin, a protein that binds and neutralises myostatin, a negative regulator of muscle mass.[3][2] A later cell study reported that YK11 up-regulates additional factors in cultured cells, and a 2023 paper reported that YK11 induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, which Grokipedia describes as occurring in the hippocampus.[10][11][2] These are laboratory findings and have not been shown in humans.

Grokipedia adds that YK-11 enhances osteoblast differentiation and Akt signalling in cell lines, and its chemical name describes a 19-norpregnane backbone, which is why some forum users and commentators say it resembles a steroid more than a non-steroidal SARM.[2][2][12]

Most pharmacokinetic work is from anti-doping research: mass spectrometric characterisation, equine metabolism after oral dosing (which detected the parent compound and phase I metabolites in plasma and urine) and detection in horse mane hair.[13][14][5] A validation study screening 60 dietary supplements purchased online in 2020 found undisclosed MK-677 and YK-11 in some products.[15]

Human safety data are absent. Health Canada states that SARM-containing bodybuilding products can pose serious risks including heart attack, stroke and liver damage, and that long-term effects are unknown.[1] One forum poster, replying to a user with health problems after SARMs, said YK-11's structure resembles an oral methylated steroid, and another poster reported side effects from a cycle that he said were not worth the modest results.[12][16]

YK-11 is a steroidal compound: according to Grokipedia, its chemical name is (17alpha,20E)-17,20-[(1-methoxyethylidene)bis(oxy)]-3-oxo-19-norpregna-4,20-diene-21-carboxylic acid methyl ester, molecular formula C25H34O6, with a molecular weight of about 430.5. Its orthoester group can hydrolyse in acid.[2] Grokipedia is AI-generated and was used only for these structural details, which should be checked against primary chemistry sources.

YK-11 was reported in 2011 by Kanno and colleagues, with a 2013 Biological and Pharmaceutical Bulletin paper on follistatin expression and myogenic differentiation.[2][3] Detection of the compound in doping samples and in supplements followed, with analytical papers appearing from 2017 onwards.[9][13][15]

Health Canada issued a 2022 warning naming YK-11 (myostine), and WADA lists SARMs as prohibited at all times.[1][4] The anti-doping literature includes a 2024 letter on detection of YK-11 in a doping control sample.[9]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: On T Nation, YK-11 is described as an untested SARM of steroid-like structure, a compound with serious potential, or a compound that did nothing for the poster; one participant said it did not give notable results and was not worth the side effects.[12][17][18][19][16] Another poster said a friend uses it because it shares a base structure with DHT, and a poster asked whether it is acceptable to combine every SARM including untested ones.[20][21]

lore.intro: YK-11 is discussed on forums as a steroid-like SARM that supposedly acts as a myostatin inhibitor, with mixed user reports.[18][19][16]
